faqs.q: Iguanas have taken over our Key West pool deck — what is realistic?
faqs.a: A managed population, honestly pursued. Key West iguanas are fully established; removal from your property is lawful and encouraged by FWC — they are Prohibited species, never to be relocated — and a focused removal plus burrow filling at the seawall and trimming of poolside feeding plants drops deck sightings dramatically. They will never be zero on an island where they swim between properties, and we will not pretend otherwise; the goal is your deck back, and that is achievable in a program of a few visits.

Key West.wildlife_intro:
Key West is its own ecosystem — a two-by-four-mile island of conch houses, wild chickens, and a famously tolerant wildlife culture at the end of the Overseas Highway. The protected Key deer are up the road on Big Pine; here the residents are iguanas (established, sunning on every seawall and pool deck), raccoons in the Old Town attics, roof rats in the palms, and the city's feral chickens, which are a civic institution and not a service item. Old Town's wooden conch houses, many raised and shuttered, are exclusion craftwork.

Wooden-house sealing in Key West is carpentry: eyebrow houses and Dade County pine take fitted work, and hurricane shutters and Bahama awnings create their own animal architecture to audit. Iguana removal is standard island practice here — removal on your property, humanely, never relocated — with pool-deck and seawall burrow management as the lasting half. Chickens get a smile and a referral to the city's own policies; we do not trap the mascots.

faqs.q: A raccoon is living on our Marathon houseboat — how is that handled?
faqs.a: Dockside, and by exclusion as much as trapping. Liveaboard raccoons commute from shore trash and mangrove cover; we trap the resident, then harden the boat's access — line and fender gaps at the dock, food storage sealed, companionway discipline — and coordinate with the harbor on the trash side, because a marina's raccoons are a system, not a boat problem. Traps are checked daily even on the water, and natives are released ashore on site or within Monroe County under the 40-acre permission rule where applicable.

faqs.q: What do I do about Muscovy ducks around my Key Largo home?
faqs.a: Feral Muscovy ducks are handled under the federal Control Order: a landowner, or our crew with the landowner's permission, may control them on the property without a federal or state permit, but captured Muscovy ducks may never be released elsewhere — relocation is illegal for this species. Traps are checked at least every 24 hours and any non-target bird is released on site. We will explain the lawful options for your property before any work starts.

Key Largo.wildlife_intro:
In Key Largo, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — island communities linked by the Overseas Highway, plus remote mainland Everglades — and features such as Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, Everglades National Park, Bahia Honda State Park, National Key Deer Refuge keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so Key Largo jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.

faqs.q: Key deer keep eating our Big Pine garden — what can we legally do?
faqs.a: Fence them out, and that is nearly the whole list. Key deer are federally Endangered; feeding, harming, or harassing one is a federal offense, and the refuge's guidance is the law of the island: deer-proof fencing around plantings you value, no intentional feeding ever, dogs managed, and extra care driving at dawn and dusk. Deer will sample unfenced landscaping forever — that is the bargain of living in their refuge. Our work stops at the fence advice and the raccoon in your attic; the deer themselves belong to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

Big Pine Key.wildlife_intro:
Big Pine Key is the Key deer's home — the National Key Deer Refuge covers much of the island, the deer wander every street under a famous reduced speed limit, and No Name Key adds its off-grid fringe. Living here means the deer are neighbors by federal law: feeding them is illegal, fencing debates are civic sport, and no wildlife company has any business offering deer anything but distance. The service work is raccoons, roof rats, and iguanas in the island's stilt homes, and marsh rabbits and protected birds as scenery.

Deer-aware practice defines Big Pine: inspections note deer fencing and gates, and our advice respects the refuge rules — deer fencing that excludes deer from gardens is a homeowner's lawful choice built to spec, while feeding or harassing deer is not. Iguana removal is standard Keys practice. For the stilt homes, under-house exclusion is the craft, done in pine-rockland surroundings where tortoises do not live — the Keys have their own protected cast, and the box turtles and deer get the same referral respect as the mainland's listed species.
